# Results

## Reservoirs mark, but do not make, irrigated vulnerability

Across the matched design (21 dammed vs 244 control subcuencas, effective control sample ≈91
after entropy balancing), dammed basins contain
roughly 4.6 times more cropland than matched controls, a mean of
11.1% of basin area versus 2.4% (@fig-area, panel a). This gap, however, is a
*siting* signature: it is present and stable across the entire 2000–2024 record, with
dammed and control trajectories evolving in parallel through the 2010-onset megadrought
(dashed line). A dynamic event study confirms this. The dammed × year coefficients on
cropland area are jointly flat before 2009 (Wald $p = 0.68$) and show no divergence after the
drought onset (@fig-area, panel b). Reservoirs mark where irrigated agriculture already
was; they do not detectably expand it or change how it responds to drought.

```{r}
#| label: fig-area
#| fig-cap: "Observed irrigated-area dynamics in dammed versus matched-control basins. (a) Weighted mean cropland area (% of basin, MapBiomas class 18); dammed basins hold ~4.6x more cropland (11.1% vs 2.4% of basin area) but trajectories are parallel. (b) Dynamic event study (dammed x year, reference 2009): flat pre-trends and no post-megadrought divergence; shaded band is the 95% confidence interval (coefficient +/- 1.96 SE). Dashed line, 2010 megadrought onset."
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("../../results/figures/fig_area_did.png")
```

## No operational reservoir effect survives once siting is matched out

We probe the operational vulnerability mechanism with four independent estimators (@tbl-main):
two cross-sectional doubly-robust matched ATTs, namely net irrigated-area expansion
($-0.69$ ha km^-2^, 95% CI $[-2.4, 1.1]$) and reservoir evapotranspiration buffering
($-0.014$ d log ET / d SPEI, $[-0.065, 0.037]$), and forcing-interacted
difference-in-differences slope gaps on the observed area and ET panels, in which the
deficit dose is the meteorological SPEI rather than calendar time (so year fixed effects
absorb the common megadrought shock and the estimand is the differential deficit-to-impact
*slope*). Because the treatment is effectively time-invariant (18 of 24 reservoirs predate
the record), this within-unit, forcing-based design is the only defensible dynamic
identification; inference uses randomization of treatment within climate × aridity strata
(~21 treated clusters).

Under the design's primary inference, no estimate indicates an operational effect
(@fig-forest, @tbl-main). Three of the four straddle zero outright: net irrigated-area
expansion, and the slope gaps for irrigated area ($p_{\text{perm}} = 0.91$) and orchard ET
($p_{\text{perm}} = 0.24$). The whole-basin ET slope gap is the exception, and we treat it
explicitly rather than fold it silently into the nulls. Its cluster-robust interval is positive
and excludes zero ($+0.048$, $[0.026, 0.070]$); however, it fails the design's pre-specified
randomization inference ($p_{\text{perm}} = 0.11$) and, decisively, its dynamic event study
shows strongly non-parallel pre-trends ($p \approx 10^{-10}$). The panel is therefore confounded
(whole-basin MODIS ET is contaminated by residual aridity over sparsely vegetated, barren land),
so neither its point estimate nor its cluster-robust interval is interpretable, and for the
same reason it is the one outcome we exclude from the equivalence bounding below. Two facts keep
this exception from rescuing a buffering narrative: taken at face value the estimate points
toward *vulnerability* (a steeper deficit-to-impact slope), not buffering; and the cleaner
orchard-ET stratum and the cross-sectional ET-buffering ATT both straddle zero. Across the
interpretable outcomes, then, no panel shows the positive slope the vulnerability mechanism
predicts nor the negative slope operational buffering would produce: conditional on siting, the
operational reservoir effect brackets zero.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-main
#| tbl-cap: "Reservoir-effect estimates across estimators. Cross-sectional doubly-robust matched ATTs and forcing-interacted DiD slope gaps (treat:SPEI). DiD rows are judged by randomization-inference p-values (p), the design's primary inference at ~21 clusters; cluster-robust CIs are shown for completeness and over-reject here. A positive estimate would indicate induced-demand vulnerability; a negative one, operational buffering. *Whole-basin ET fails its event-study pre-trend test (p approximately 1e-10): its cluster-robust CI excludes zero but the panel is confounded by barren-land aridity, so it is labelled confounded and excluded from the equivalence bounds (Table 2)."
#| echo: false
tab <- data.table::fread("../../results/tables/table_main_results.csv")
# Whole-basin ET fails its event-study pre-trends (p~1e-10): the cluster CI excludes zero but the
# panel is confounded (barren-land aridity), so it is neither a clean null nor an interpretable
# effect. Label it honestly rather than "null" (the source verdict is permutation-judged).
tab[outcome == "Whole-basin ET", verdict := "confounded*"]
knitr::kable(tab[, .(Group = group, Outcome = outcome, Estimand = estimand,
                     Estimate = round(estimate, 3),
                     `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.3g, %.3g]", ci_lo, ci_hi),
                     p = ifelse(is.na(p), "-", sprintf("%.2f", p)), Verdict = verdict)])
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-forest
#| fig-cap: "Standardized dammed-versus-control effect across the four estimators. DiD rows are standardized via their randomization-inference p-value (the design's primary inference), so whole-basin ET (cluster-significant but permutation-null and pre-trend-confounded) sits within the bounds; cross-sectional ATTs use estimate/SE. Horizontal bars span +/-1.96 standardized units (the 95% reference interval); dotted lines mark +/-1.96."
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("../../results/figures/fig_convergent_null.png")
```

## Sensitivity to aridity adjustment

Dammed basins are systematically more arid than controls, and the matched set does not fully
remove this: baseline aridity remains imbalanced after weighting (standardized mean difference
≈$0.17$, above the $0.1$ target), so the doubly-robust adjustment for aridity is load-bearing
rather than a cosmetic mop-up. Because dammed basins are the more arid, residual under-control
biases *toward* apparent vulnerability, which makes the nulls conservative. Functional form
matters and we report it: in the ecological-proxy transmission-slope analysis the dammed-versus-
control estimate falls from $+0.33$ under linear aridity adjustment to $+0.11$ once a quadratic
aridity term is added, and in the irrigation-specific stratum it collapses to ≈$0$
($0.08 \rightarrow 0.01$). The apparent steepening is therefore largely a water-limitation/aridity
artifact (consistent with the siting interpretation), but the same sensitivity means estimates
that rely on linear aridity control should be read as functional-form-dependent, and we treat the
curvature-robust values as the conservative reference.

## Bounding the null: what the design can rule out

A null is only informative against a stated effect size, so we convert each non-result into a
bound via equivalence testing (two one-sided tests) and a minimum detectable effect (MDE)
built from the permutation-null spread (@tbl-equiv). We bound the four interpretable outcomes
(streamflow ITT and downstream, irrigated-area DiD, orchard-ET DiD); whole-basin ET is excluded
because its pre-trends fail, so an equivalence interval on a confounded estimate would be
meaningless. The streamflow design has the most power:
it can detect a buffering effect that attenuates SPEI→SSI transmission by ≳46% of the baseline
slope (ITT MDE $0.27$ against a baseline transmission of $0.59$; downstream-only MDE $0.31$
against its $0.53$ baseline, ≳58%). Here "baseline" is the untreated (control) SPEI→SSI slope from
the fixed-effects model (@tbl-equiv), which is distinct from, and should not be confused with,
the raw per-gauge mean transmission of downstream gauges ($0.599$) reported for the placebo
comparability check (@tbl-placebo). No outcome's 90%
interval falls inside its pre-specified negligible region (±25% of baseline), so we do *not*
claim formal statistical equivalence to zero (with ~21 treated clusters the design can exclude
only **large** operational effects, not small ones). A policy-relevant buffer of 20–45% of
baseline transmission is *not* excluded. The causal weight of the null therefore rests on the
within-basin placebo below, not on equivalence: the design excludes only large operational
effects, and the placebo indicates that the residual apparent attenuation is selection rather
than regulation.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-equiv
#| tbl-cap: "Equivalence / minimum-detectable-effect bounds on the headline nulls. Observed slope gap, MDE (smallest effect detectable at 80% power from the permutation-null SD), the 90% (TOST) interval, and whether it lies within the negligible region (+/-25% of baseline). 'baseline' is the untreated (control) SPEI->SSI / SPEI->impact transmission slope from the fixed-effects model. No outcome is formally equivalent to zero; the streamflow design rules out attenuations larger than ~46-58% of baseline transmission."
#| echo: false
eq <- data.table::fread("../../results/tables/table_equivalence.csv")
knitr::kable(eq[, .(Outcome = outcome,
                    Observed = round(observed, 3),
                    MDE = round(mde, 3),
                    `90% CI` = sprintf("[%.3g, %.3g]", ci90_lo, ci90_hi),
                    `Equiv. to 0?` = ifelse(equivalent, "yes", "no"),
                    `p_perm` = round(p_perm, 2))])
```

To confirm that this null is informative rather than merely underpowered (that the design could
detect a true effect of the relevant order), we ran a positive control on the streamflow estimator
(@tbl-poscontrol). Injecting a known buffering slope into the treated downstream units, the
estimator recovers it almost exactly (a $-0.30$ injection yields $-0.47$ on top of the $-0.17$
baseline), the no-injection case is correctly *not* flagged ($p_{\text{perm}} = 0.48$), and
randomization inference detects the effect once the total slope reaches ≈$-0.47$
($p_{\text{perm}} = 0.014$), with $-0.62$ strongly detected ($p_{\text{perm}} = 0.001$). The
design therefore has the power to reveal a large operational buffering effect where one exists, so
its failure to find one is evidence of absence at that magnitude (consistent with the MDE above)
rather than blindness. This positive control validates the streamflow estimator specifically; the
irrigated-area and ET nulls are not independently power-validated, their minimum detectable
effects being large (for irrigated area, far above any plausible effect; @tbl-equiv), and rest on
the placebo and the conservative direction of the aridity bias rather than on their own power.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-poscontrol
#| tbl-cap: "Positive control on the streamflow estimator. A known buffering slope (beta_injected; negative = buffering) is added to treated downstream units; the estimator recovers it (recovered = baseline -0.17 + beta), the no-effect case is not flagged, and randomization inference detects the effect once it exceeds the minimum detectable effect."
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(data.table::fread("../../results/tables/table_positive_control.csv"))
```

## The apparent buffering is reservoir siting, not regulation

The preceding nulls use vegetation and ET proxies. We obtain the same answer on the direct,
vegetation-independent availability outcome (streamflow), and, uniquely here, can show *why* a
naive analysis would mislead. From CR2 daily gauge records (2000–2020) we build a 12-month
Standardized Streamflow Index (SSI-12) and test whether meteorological drought (SPEI-12)
propagates less strongly to streamflow drought in dammed than in matched-control basins
(@fig-streamflow). Dammed basins do show a flatter SPEI→SSI transmission, the visual signature
of buffering (@fig-streamflow, panel a). But this apparent attenuation **(i)** does not survive
randomization inference (intent-to-treat slope gap $-0.18$, cluster $p = 0.03$ but
$p_{\text{perm}} = 0.39$), and **(ii)** is present just as strongly at gauges located *upstream*
of the dam (which are physically unregulated) as at downstream gauges
($-0.20$ vs $-0.16$; @fig-streamflow, panel b). There is no downstream-versus-upstream
dose-response, the signature a genuine regulation effect would require. The flatter slope is
therefore a property of *where* reservoirs are sited (arid, hydrogeologically distinct basins),
not of the reservoirs themselves.

The siting interpretation is confirmed by the way the signal behaves across the aridity
gradient. The national "buffering" slope gap ($-0.16$ to $-0.20$) **collapses to ≈ $-0.03$ once
the comparison is made within climate region**, the textbook signature of a between-region
confound, in which arid treated basins are contrasted against a control pool spanning the whole
wet→dry gradient. In the high-supply south, where buffering should be easiest to detect, the
downstream and upstream gaps are statistically identical ($-0.036$ vs $-0.034$) and both
indistinguishable from zero (southern downstream $p_{\text{perm}} = 0.78$). Splitting by region
thus both kills the signal and equalizes the upstream and downstream reaches, two independent
confirmations that the attenuation is the aridity gradient, not regulation. Because the
upstream-of-dam comparison is unavailable for any vegetation outcome, streamflow provides the
cleanest within-design falsification: the effect a naive dammed-versus-control or calendar-time
analysis would report is siting, not regulation.

The placebo assumes upstream and downstream reaches are hydrologically comparable, which we test
directly (@tbl-placebo). Upstream gauges do sit higher than downstream ones (mean $1.0$ vs $0.46$
km), and gauge elevation is not innocuous. Among undammed control gauges the SPEI→SSI
transmission slope declines by $0.21$ per kilometre of elevation ($p < 0.001$). The placebo
nonetheless holds, for two reasons. First, the *raw* transmission slopes of upstream and
downstream treated gauges are nearly identical ($0.565$ vs $0.599$), so the elevation difference
does not produce a transmission-regime gap of the size at issue. Second, the apparent buffering is
if anything *stronger* upstream ($-0.20$) than downstream ($-0.16$), the opposite of what
regulation, which acts only downstream, would produce. We cannot claim the reaches are perfectly
interchangeable, and a residual elevation/regime component remains a caveat, but neither the raw
slopes nor the direction of the gap supports a regulation effect masked by elevation.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-placebo
#| tbl-cap: "Upstream/downstream placebo comparability. Upstream gauges are higher than downstream, and gauge elevation predicts the transmission slope among undammed controls (-0.21 per +1000 m), yet upstream and downstream treated gauges have nearly identical raw transmission slopes, so the equal up/down attenuation is not an elevation artifact."
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(data.table::fread("../../results/tables/table_placebo_check.csv"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-streamflow
#| fig-cap: "Streamflow buffering is reservoir siting, not regulation. (a) SPEI-12 to SSI-12 transmission for dammed versus matched-control basins (downstream gauges); lines are weighted least-squares fits and shaded bands are 95% confidence intervals; dammed basins show a flatter slope, the apparent buffering. (b) Differential slope (treat:SPEI; <0 = buffering) for intent-to-treat, downstream-only, and the upstream-only placebo; horizontal bars are 95% confidence intervals (estimate +/- 1.96 cluster-robust SE), annotated with randomization-inference p-values. All are permutation-null, and the upstream placebo (above-dam, unregulated) is as strong as downstream, so the attenuation is siting/aridity, not the dam."
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("../../results/figures/fig_streamflow.png")
```

## Storage declines without a loss of buffering capacity

If reservoirs neither buffer nor amplify drought operationally, the relevant change under the
megadrought is in how much water is available to store (@fig-storage). Over 2005–2024 the entire
storage band drifts downward in step: annual peak storage declines by $-1.3$ percentage points
of capacity per year ($p = 0.013$) and the annual trough falls almost identically ($-1.2$ pp
yr^-1^, $p < 10^{-4}$), while the seasonal amplitude is statistically unchanged ($-0.06$ pp
yr^-1^, $p = 0.91$). A band that drops without narrowing is consistent with a supply-side level
shift rather than a degraded buffer, which would compress the amplitude; reservoirs still convert
meteorological surplus into storage as efficiently as before. We caution that this storage trend
is descriptive (a pooled within-reservoir trend with no control group or naturalized-inflow
series), so it cannot by itself distinguish declining inflow from rising demand-side drawdown.
The most direct demand proxy available to us weighs against the demand explanation, however:
irrigated area in dammed basins shows no expansion over the period (stable, parallel trajectories,
@fig-area; differential-expansion ATT indistinguishable from zero, @tbl-main), so a growing
consumptive footprint is not evident as a driver of the storage decline, though a compositional
shift toward more water-intensive perennials could raise per-area use without enlarging area.
Read alongside Chile's documented aridification, the pattern is therefore more consistent with a
falling water supply than with any loss of storage or buffering capacity, and on that reading the
operational case for expanding storage as drought protection is weak
[@li_diminishing_2023; @wang_reservoir_2024].

```{r}
#| label: fig-storage
#| fig-cap: "Storage declines without a loss of buffering capacity. (a) Cross-reservoir annual storage band, peak and trough percent-of-capacity (mean line; shaded bands are the interquartile range across reservoirs), drifts downward over 2005-2024 with roughly parallel trend lines: the whole band shifts while seasonal amplitude is unchanged. (b) Per-year trend slope of peak, trough, and amplitude (reservoir fixed effects); error bars are 95% confidence intervals (estimate +/- 1.96 cluster-robust SE): peak and trough both decline while amplitude brackets zero, consistent with a supply-side level decline rather than a refill/buffer degradation. Descriptive: pooled within-reservoir trend, no control group."
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("../../results/figures/fig_storage_band.png")
```
